primary_topics: Closing remarks at the FLP-MBF Professorial Chair lecture by Dean Gemy Lito Festin at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP), May 12, 2018

The Writ of Prosperity proposal: CJP urges Dean Festin and PALS to craft detailed Rules of Procedure for a Writ of Prosperity -- following the Colombian Supreme Court's Tutelary Rules as a model -- to give judicial enforceability to economic rights

CJP's personal story: the UST Dominican priest interview (failed the Trinity question, answered 'Susmariosep!'), leading to FEU, Fr. Michael Nolan, Catholic lay leadership, and ultimately the Pontifical Council for the Laity -- from Catholic ignoramus to the Pope's highest lay advisory council
PUP as CJP's sentimental school: site of his first law office; hotbed of activism; connected to his founding of NUSP; where he met Leni Carpio
sub_topics: Dean Festin's lecture: 'Tutelary Rules Principle as Legal Tool for Easing Economic Rights' Access to Justice in the Philippines'; one of the best in the FLP-MBF lecture series; references Colombia's Supreme Court approach to enforcing economic rights
Honorarium presented: P100,000 check less P10,000 withholding tax remitted to BIR; Dean Festin's piece to appear in FLP-MBF Coffee Table Book

Political vs. economic rights: economic rights in the Constitution are not self-executing; need enabling legislation; contrast with Bill of Rights (self-executing political/civil rights); reason: Constitutions born from political-independence struggles; even the US Bill of Rights born from Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty or give me death'

Filipino polls: most urgent concerns are poverty, jobs, high prices -- liberation from poverty; 'Of what use indeed is the freedom to travel if we cannot fill our stomachs? Of what use is the freedom of information, if we cannot quench our thirst for potable water?'

Writ of Prosperity: modeled on the Colombian Tutelary Rules; new Rules of Procedure from the SC under its constitutional rule-making power; proposed to be crafted by PALS (Sedfrey Candelaria at Ateneo as sympathetic president); to be supported by FLP and Metrobank Foundation

Concurrent constitutional amendment proposal: amend the Constitution to include 'the right to prosperity and the corollary right against poverty' -- timely given current constitutional amendment efforts

PUP sentimentality: formerly Philippine College of Commerce (1901); transformed into university by activist educators led by late Dr. Nemesio Prudente; CJP's first law office was on Ramon Magsaysay Boulevard near PUP; was planning to run for Congress in the University Belt district until his wife vetoed it

NUSP and PUP connection: PUP as hotbed of activism; CJP organized NUSP more than 50 years ago; Catholic schools like Ateneo, La Salle, St. Theresa and St. Scholastica initially didn't participate in non-Catholic student organizations; NUSP 'crossed the cloisters and got the collegialas into the mainstream student movements' -- bonus: met Leni Carpio because of NUSP

PUP FLP scholars: Jun Dexter Roxas, Ma. Vida Malaya Villarico, Rexlyn Anne Evora -- 3 of 21 scholarships; only Ateneo de Manila surpassed PUP with 4 scholars; Ms. Evora was also a dissertation contest finalist

stances.claim: Economic rights in the Philippine Constitution are not self-executing -- they require implementing legislation and cannot by themselves be enforced by the judiciary. This is a structural constitutional design flaw rooted in the historical accident that all Philippine constitutions (from Malolos to 1987) were drafted during political-independence struggles, making political and civil rights the dominant register. The Writ of Prosperity is the proposed judicial remedy for this structural gap.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-design-flaw diagnosis: the non-self-executing status of economic rights is not a permanent feature but a historical accident that can be corrected by SC rule-making power

stances.claim: The SC has constitutional authority to promulgate new rules of procedure -- as it did for the Writ of Amparo, Habeas Data, and Kalikasan -- and should use this power to create a Writ of Prosperity, modeled on Colombia's Tutelary Rules, to give judicial enforceability to economic rights. This does not require a constitutional amendment (though CJP proposes that too, concurrently).
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-making-power argument: the SC's constitutional authority to promulgate rules as the vehicle for the Writ of Prosperity, bypassing the need for legislative action
stances.confidence: asserted as a specific actionable proposal

stances.claim: From failing the Trinity question at UST to becoming the Pope's sole Filipino lay adviser at the Pontifical Council for the Laity -- 'from being a Catholic ignoramus... I graduated to the highest lay advisory council of the Pope in the Vatican.' Disappointments and defeats are opportunities and challenges to achieve victory later in life. Poverty and ignorance are not barriers to success.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-reversal narrative: the UST rejection as the setup for the Vatican appointment -- the most improbable success arc as an inspiration for PUP's poor students

notable_anecdotes: The UST Trinity anecdote: a Dominican priest offered CJP a scholarship contingent on answering three questions. Q1: How many Gods? A: One. Q2: How many persons in one God? A: Three. Q3: Name them. CJP muttered 'Susmariosep!' The priest boomed 'Wrong!' -- ending his hope of entering the oldest university in the country. CJP went to FEU instead.

The NUSP-Leni-Carpio bonus: NUSP 'crossed the cloisters and got the collegialas into the mainstream student movements. This historic turn was a bonus for me -- it was because of the NUSP that I met the gentle Scholastican, Elenita Carpio, who later became my wife.'

The Catholic ignoramus arc: from the UST Trinity failure (didn't know the three persons of the Holy Trinity) to the Second Plenary Council (1991) to Pope John Paul II's appointment to the Pontifical Council for the Laity (1996-2002): 'I graduated to the highest lay advisory council of the Pope in the Vatican.' The moral: 'we should take disappointments and defeats as opportunities and challenges to achieve victory later in life.'

The First Law Office near PUP: CJP's first law office was on Ramon Magsaysay Boulevard 'very near the vehicular bridge crossing the railroad, less than one kilometer away' from PUP. He was planning to run for Congress in the University Belt district 'until the idea was vetoed by my dear wife who did not want any partisan political post for me, or for our children.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered May 12, 2018 as closing remarks at the FLP-MBF Professorial Chair lecture at PUP, this speech by CJP presents Dean Gemy Lito Festin his P100,000 honorarium (less P10,000 withholding tax) and announces his piece on the 'Tutelary Rules Principle' -- 'one of the best lectures I have heard since the FLP-MBF lecture series started' -- will feature in the FLP-MBF Coffee Table Book. He introduces three reactors (Atty. De la Cruz-Cada of IBP, Judge Villarosa, and Atty. Bayobay of the Ombudsman). The substantive argument: economic rights in the Constitution are not self-executing -- rooted in the historical accident that all Philippine constitutions were born from political-independence struggles ('Give me liberty or give me death'), making political and civil rights the dominant register while economic rights were left as 'mere ideals and aspirations' requiring implementing laws. Of what use is freedom of travel if one cannot fill one's stomach? The proposal: a Writ of Prosperity, modeled on Colombia's Tutelary Rules, promulgated by the SC under its constitutional rule-making power (same power used for the Writ of Amparo, Habeas Data and Kalikasan) -- with Dean PALS President Sedfrey Candelaria of Ateneo called upon to spearhead the Rules drafting, and FLP and MBF pledging support; plus a concurrent constitutional amendment to include the right to prosperity and the corollary right against poverty. He then indulges PUP's activist spirit by noting his sentimental connection (first law office on Ramon Magsaysay Boulevard near PUP; planning to run for Congress in the University Belt until his wife vetoed it; NUSP founding, which -- bonus -- led to meeting Leni Carpio). He announces three PUP FLP scholars (Roxas, Villarico, Evora). He closes with his Catholic ignoramus arc: failed the UST Trinity question ('Susmariosep!'); enrolled at FEU; met Fr. Michael Nolan; attended the Second Plenary Council (1991); appointed by Pope John Paul II to the 30-member Pontifical Council for the Laity (1996-2002) -- 'the only Filipino lay member.' Moral: 'Poverty and ignorance are not barriers to success. They can be overcome.'
